title: The English break
hookLine: Henry VIII leaves Rome; Catholics and Protestants were both martyred in England

lines: THE KING'S FRIEND, IN THE TOWER.
cards: Thomas More had been the king's friend, and then his Lord Chancellor. Now he's in the Tower of London, and all he has to do to walk out is swear an oath. Others around him have sworn.
His own family begs him to. He's a lawyer; he knows every way around a sentence. He won't swear it, and he won't say why.
Today, the English break, a story where faithful people died on both sides.

teach.h: THE KING CUTS TIES WITH ROME.
teach.b: First, the break. King Henry the Eighth wanted his marriage to Catherine of Aragon declared invalid. The pope would not grant it.

So the king and Parliament cut the English Church off from Rome and named the king its supreme head on earth. Next, the cost to Catholics. Oaths were required, and refusing put a person in the king's prisons.
Thomas More refused, and so did John Fisher, a bishop. Both were tried for treason and beheaded. More is remembered as saying on the scaffold that he died the king's good servant, but God's first.
The Catholic Church honors both as saints. Then, the turn.
Henry had sent some Protestants to the fire too, but under his daughter Mary, a Catholic who restored ties to Rome, Protestants were burned for heresy in far greater numbers.
Among them was Thomas Cranmer, the archbishop behind the English Book of Common Prayer; Anglicans remember him and others as martyrs.
Under the next queen, Elizabeth, it turned again: Catholic priests were hanged, among them the Jesuit Edmund Campion, whom the Catholic Church honors as a saint. Last, what they shared.

The apostles' words in Acts could be said of every one of them; in the Douay-Rheims they read, "We ought to obey God, rather than men." They disagreed about what God asked, and agreed it was worth dying for.
Catholics and Anglicans today can honor their own martyrs without pretending the others weren't sincere.

how: The Catholic Church keeps feast days for Saints Thomas More, John Fisher and the English martyrs; the Church of England also remembers its own martyrs of the period, and Catholics and Anglicans today meet in formal dialogue.

games.q: the English break — tap the pairs.
p: named supreme head of the English Church
the king's good servant, but God's first

s: only Catholics died for their faith in that era of England
Protestants were burned, above all under Mary; under Henry and Elizabeth, Catholics died too.
the break began when the pope refused to annul the king's marriage
the king and Parliament then cut ties with Rome.
Thomas More swore the oath in the end
he refused, and he was beheaded.

games.q: you're Thomas More in the Tower. one oath and you walk free. your family begs you. what do you do?
o: swear it, and keep your private reservations.
refuse the oath, and keep silent about your reasons.
escape by night to the continent.
games.why: More refused and kept his reasons to himself as long as he could; he was beheaded, and the Church honors him as a saint.

practice: Bring to mind a few names from today, Thomas More, John Fisher, Thomas Cranmer, Edmund Campion, and hold them side by side, not as teams.

Then widen it to anyone, anywhere, who has suffered for refusing to say what they didn't believe. If you pray, commend them all to God's mercy, the ones you agree with and the ones you don't; if not, simply remember them.

wordCard.voice: Thomas More. The king's chancellor who refused the oath of supremacy and was beheaded, one of many who died on both sides of England's break with Rome. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: martyrs on both sides. A conviction across from yours can still be sincere. Go gently.
